name: Card grid for heterogeneous telemetry
problem: An authenticated home must show many unlike signals (metrics, tips, announcements, tasks) without collapsing them into one monolithic chart or endless list.
worksWhen: Signals differ in type and update cadence, so each card can own one job
Users return frequently and scan rather than read
Cards can be collapsed, reordered, or gated by eligibility instead of shown as empty shells
failsWhen: Every card gets equal visual weight so nothing reads as primary
Cards multiply without curation and push key signals below the fold
The surface is a focused operator console where one dense table would serve better

name: Resume-in-progress leads the home
problem: Returning users of creation or consumption tools want to continue prior work, but many homes lead with discovery or marketing modules instead.
worksWhen: Return visits dominate over first visits
Recent objects are unambiguous and safe to surface
A recents lane can sit beside starred or favorited lanes for different return jobs
failsWhen: The product is session-less so recency has no meaning
Recents expose sensitive content on shared screens
New-user onboarding needs the first screen more than continuation does

name: Primary table with side diagnostics
problem: Operators need object-level work (rows) and account-level awareness (quotas, compliance, status) at the same time without switching pages.
worksWhen: A content or order table is the main workspace and side panels carry persistent constraints
Compliance or quota indicators must stay visible while acting on rows
Filters live above the table instead of hidden in advanced search
failsWhen: Side panels grow into a second competing workspace
The account signals update rarely enough that a settings page suffices
Small viewports force the panels to stack and bury the table

name: Editable KPI canvas for expert homes
problem: Expert operators have divergent priorities, so a fixed KPI home either overwhelms some users or starves others.
worksWhen: Users are experts who know which metrics matter to them
Tile units, movement, and resizing are documented first-class behaviors
Scope and time controls stay persistent in the top bar
failsWhen: Casual users face a blank or misconfigured canvas
Personal customization fragments shared team awareness
Permission gates leave most operators unable to edit what they see

name: Mobile home as summary, not console
problem: Porting a full operator console to mobile produces cramped controls, so mobile homes must choose a narrower job.
worksWhen: The mobile surface is an at-a-glance summary with deep links to focused screens
Bottom tabs carry primary destinations and one launcher covers quick actions
Owners prepare a phone view instead of letting desktop layouts reflow
failsWhen: Creation or configuration tasks are forced into the mobile shell
Uniform portrait stacking flattens hierarchy without a prepared phone layout
The summary hides so much that operators must always switch to desktop

name: Safety controls one layer deep
problem: Hosts and moderators need intervention controls during live events, but burying them in settings makes response too slow while inlining all of them crowds the surface.
worksWhen: A dedicated panel or menu groups all safety actions one tap from the main view
Roles (host, co-host, moderator) have documented capability differences
High-frequency actions (block, slow mode, mute) are closest to the content they act on
failsWhen: Critical safety rules hide behind multiple navigation layers
The toolbar accumulates every feature until scanning fails under pressure
Role differences are so intricate that operators misremember who can act

name: Job verbs over abstract slogans
problem: Public homepages for tools drift into abstract benefit language that fails to tell visitors what they can actually do.
worksWhen: Capabilities are named with the user's own working verbs
The hero states one end-to-end workflow promise before feature detail
Advanced power is expressed through a few memorable verbs instead of a matrix
failsWhen: The audience buys on brand feeling rather than capability
Verb lists grow so long they become the matrix they replaced
Enterprise buyers need proof and compliance language more than verbs

name: Chaptered scroll story for long homepages
problem: Broad platforms need long homepages, but an undifferentiated scroll of feature cards loses visitors midway.
worksWhen: The page divides into a small set of named narrative chapters
Repeated CTA returns follow each major proof section
Format or audience switches act as visible waypoints
failsWhen: Chapters multiply until the page becomes a sitemap
Each chapter repeats the same layout so waypoints stop registering
A focused single-product page would answer the visitor faster

name: Working canvas as hero proof
problem: Builder products claim control and power, but generic mockups leave the claim unproven on the first screen.
worksWhen: The hero shows the real working canvas with navigation, layers, and publish actions visible
Realistic interface chrome carries the proof instead of abstract illustration
One believable scenario with domain-specific data anchors credibility
failsWhen: The product UI is too dense to read at hero scale
A staged screenshot drifts from the shipped product and erodes trust
The audience is non-technical and reads the canvas as complexity

name: Suite homepage as routing layer
problem: Multi-product suites overload a single persuasion page; visitors with different intents need different destinations fast.
worksWhen: The homepage treats itself as a discovery map with one sharp line per product
Roles, use cases, or team entry points widen relevance without duplicating pages
Platform, solution, and learning routes stay separated in navigation
failsWhen: Routing tiles replace any actual persuasion so the page feels like a directory
A single flagship product deserves the hero instead of the suite
Visitors cannot tell products apart from one-line descriptions

name: Stable shell as orientation layer
problem: Dense authenticated products disorient users when navigation chrome shifts with content, especially across many destinations.
worksWhen: A persistent header and side nav stay fixed while only the content region changes
Side-nav groups expand for products that outgrow flat header navigation
Focus return and collapse behavior are specified, not left to chance
failsWhen: The shell consumes so much space that content starves on laptops
Every module invents its own shell variant and orientation breaks
A single-surface tool gains bureaucracy from a shell it does not need

name: Saved views over repeated search
problem: Operators repeat the same filtered queries daily; making them re-derive filters wastes time and invites inconsistency.
worksWhen: Filter combinations recur and deserve named, persistent views
Views appear as a visible strip or list, not buried in menus
Sorting, grouping, and column choices persist per view
failsWhen: View proliferation makes the tab strip itself unscannable
No governance exists so team views drift into private dialects
The dataset is small enough that one default view suffices
